touches.text: Owns the CC launcher (superclaude): starts Claude Code with Cairn's session contract, in its own memory-capped cgroup. WHY: Claude can OOM the box.

superclaude is Python on every box, launched by the platform shell (5.4.3.8.5), and inherits the elevation the shell settled (5.4.3.8.6): elevated PowerShell on Windows, sudo with IS_SANDBOX=1 on Linux; it never elevates itself. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator

Owns the Claude Code hooks: mail check, the turn-shape and ask scans, the gates on record writes and deletes. Anything that adapts CC specifically to Cairn goes in the CC device, and every one of CC's scripts lives here.

There is no central supervisor. Each part starts what it needs by trying to use it: sending a message starts the bus if it is down, a message arriving wakes its shim, the shim wakes its device. Many very small supervisors, each one detect-and-start. WHY: a supervisor is one more thing to keep up, and the system must come up from any part that is touched.

Declaring a new instance rotates, explicitly or implicitly: --new rotates explicitly, no flag rotates implicitly, --name overrides both. -amm Reading (superclaude is the rescue service's launcher, cairn/devices/cc/superclaude; none of these needs a folder prepared by hand): - `cairn superclaude --new` always rotates explicitly to the next undeclared n (cc_1 when cc_0 is declared, cc_2 when cc_1 is, and so on), then declares, wires and launches it. - `cairn superclaude` with no flag rotates implicitly: it starts cc_0 when cc_0 is free, and when cc_0 is taken (running) it rotates as --new does. - `cairn superclaude --name <x>` uses exactly x and overrides all of that: it declares x if absent, then launches it. - The declared folder commits through the door in the same act, so the house tree is not left dirty and crossings are not refused. - The one CC inference here: "implicitly" is read as taken (running) cc_0 means rotate, while a declared-but-stopped cc_0 is simply started. Tickets: aa05710a5124 reshapes to this; d13859e2ae46 is the implicit rotation; 0f7a8cada1ca names the next undeclared n. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

Each platform shell does two things, in order, before handing over: it elevates, then it runs Cairn's own Python on the launcher (on Windows `@python <path>\cairn ...`; on Linux the same without the @). Every decision after that is Python's; the shell holds no other logic beyond the fall-over above.

Elevation is the shell's, settled before Python starts, and nothing inside asks again. On Windows the shell runs in an elevated PowerShell. On Linux the shell sudoes the launch, with IS_SANDBOX=1 set so Claude Code accepts bypass permissions under root. WHY: the whole box is the sandbox, so elevating once at launch is simpler than elevating on request; IS_SANDBOX=1 is set on every box for that reason. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
The exceptions are client tools a device publishes:

System: a box has to name itself before any bus is up (a saveslate, an install), so the system device publishes the host's name and OS family (6.6.3.7). - akiendelllinux_cc_0 2.3.8Every device has the panes the base shim defines (17.1.3.5.2), drawn by the web server (15):
The installer verifies every host-seam on every box. It never skips one because of the box's platform.

What the waker starts outlives whoever started it (detached, or through systemd-run --user, which gives it its own memory cap and log while still deciding nothing). Restarting a shim never takes down the bus it once woke.

The only way to the inference host; anything that goes around it is an error. WHY: its two points are to find the cheapest model powerful enough for each request, and to train the graph trees on the results.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.

Tool: a complete primitive. Has users, not an owner. Owns no state of its own. May use any library, other tools included. Lives in cairn/tools/ (17). Its data for a holder lives under that holder: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/. WHY: the rule keeps encapsulation useful inside our world, so the system stays within the complexity CC can manage. Forbidding libraries would forbid opening files. -amm
Trouble: it has to be able to report when nothing else can, so a direct line makes sense for recovery (6.3.4).
`cairn start` (= cairn cairn start) brings the system up: ground loop, bus, shims. `cairn stop` takes it down.
Two callers waking the same part at once start only one: the part that binds its socket first is the only one; a second copy finds it taken and exits quietly (as the ground loop does, 5.6.4.3).
INTENTION:

In front of it sits a thin platform shell (a shell script on Linux, cairn.cmd or cairn.ps1 on Windows) with enough brains to fall over to Rescue (6.5) when it can't find Cairn's Python, or Python throws, or anything else stops the launcher. The failure throws a trouble ticket (3.4.3), and the ticket is Rescue's "read this" (6.5.3.5); a repeat increments that ticket's counter. Rescue's prompt says: at the end of proving the fix, check for more errors, to clear or fix as appropriate. WHY: trouble has to be able to report when nothing else can (2.3.7.1.3).
INTENTION:
It launches each device's cairn/devices/<device>/groundloop/pulse.py, each as its own process (5.8.3.4).
The shim always starts its device. Nothing else does.
It wakes the device when it's not running and is needed.

Install and upgrades live here: the installer machine walks the host-seam intentions, verifies each, offers what's missing, applies, re-verifies. If xyz library needs an update, this is the component that does it. Any change to what the host is goes through here (6.6.3.1.1).
Launched automatically by a failed install, start or launch, with "read this" and the trouble ticket saying what happened and what it wants to make happen. The operator can also launch it by hand.

The line is using vs changing. Any device may USE the OS's services (write a file, open a socket, start or stop its own unit with systemctl). CHANGING what the host is (installing or updating systemd unit files, packages, udev rules, cron entries) goes through Recovery. Eg Cairn restarts the bus itself; putting the bus's unit file in place goes through Recovery.

The hostname comes from the system device. It answers which box (the short hostname, lowercased) and which OS family, and nothing else in Cairn asks the OS for the hostname. Callers reach it through the client tool it publishes (2.3.7.1.5), so a box names itself on every OS, Windows included, with no bus running. - akiendelllinux_cc_0
INTENTION:
Any cairn command brings up whatever it needs, including the whole install on the very first run (6.3.2). WHY: a well designed tool should disappear in use.
The detect-and-start lives in one tool, the waker, and it sits inside connect: every client's connect is a wake attempt, so no caller can forget one. A probe watches and reports; the waker acts.

The second copy exits SILENTLY; refusing loudly has no reason behind it. A --force switch means "don't exit if another is running: kill the other and take over", for replacing a running older version with a newer one. This is the ground loop's rule; CC's reading is that it holds for every host singleton (bus, rack, a device name). - CC

More than one instance of a device is allowed: many things can be singletons or not (eg a second embeddings generator on another host when traffic is heavy). Instances have distinct names so messages route. Naming is the shim's job: the launcher asks the shim for an instance, and a shim given no name when cc_0 exists launches cc_1.
Nothing requires Akien's word for a proof to run. A proof that starts Windows processes runs without asking; no env var or standing flag gates it.
On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one. WHY: the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos).
ground_loop (machine): the heartbeat

One bus per cairn instance, not per host. Each box runs its own bus, and the buses talk to one another, so a device always talks to the bus on its own box; together they are the instance's one bus. A device runs on one box; the other boxes reach it over the buses. No box needs a full set of devices. WHY: so the instance can run several heavy tasks at once across boxes.

Has its own email account (CC's, not Igor's; credentials under ~/.cairn/devices/cc/0/, the only record). Its shim fetches the mail, since shims handle all interfacing with the outside world (5.8.3.8); CC never checks the mailbox itself.
It runs on one box, so a box that joins the instance starts no web server of its own; its devices show in the one server through the buses (5.5.3.8).
Rescue (Claude Code outside Cairn; part of Recovery, not a device of its own)
Physics: the encapsulation_holds sieve in build_inspector, a device-path check. Code in device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo except a tool foo publishes. Inside one device nothing is checked.

conflicts.text: On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one. WHY: the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos).
conflicts.ticket_says: claude is spawned in this console with inherited stdio... the exit code is claude's
conflicts.why: Outline 5.3.5.3.2 states 'On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one.' If claude inherits stdio from superclaude.py running in a user's terminal, it appears in that console. The outline's reasoning 'the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos)' suggests windows/console output should be hidden by default. However, ticket decision D3 specifies 'claude runs in THIS console with inherited stdio, as UnseenUniversity bin/superclaude.ps1 does', indicating this preserves existing behavior. The contradiction is whether inherited-stdio spawning is compatible with the outline's requirement that processes run windowless by default on Windows.
